sources.title: Lectures on the Origin and Growth of Religion as Illustrated by the Religion of the Ancient Babylonians (Hibbert Lectures, 1887)
sources.author: A. H. Sayce
sources.notes: Sayce's translation of the hemerology of the second (intercalary) Elul, a tablet from Ashurbanipal's library (W.A.I. IV 32–33), giving the god, the luck and the king's rites and restrictions for each of the 30 days of the month. A 19th-century translation: some readings ("Sabbath", "fast-day", gods' names such as Merodach, Nebo, Adar, Rimmon) are dated. Public domain.

lunar_days.name: Day 2
lunar_days.meaning: Day 2 of the Babylonian month. In the day-by-day calendar of the second Ulūlu: The two Ishtars.
lunar_days.uncertainty: From one Assyrian copy, in Ashurbanipal's library (7th century BCE), of the day-by-day calendar for the extra (second) Ulūlu, as translated by A. H. Sayce in 1887. Its rules are addressed to the king. Sayce's "Sabbath" and "fast-day" are his 1887 renderings: modern scholars read the 7th, 14th, 19th, 21st and 28th as "evil days" (ūmu lemnu) restricting the king's acts. Tablets for other months differ in details. The modern date comes from an illustrative model of the Babylonian month.

recommendations.historical_practice: Dedicated to Adad (Sayce: "Rimmon") and Ninlil. A lucky day. The king recites a penitential psalm and a litany. At night, facing the east wind, he makes his offering to Adad.

recommendations.historical_practice: A "fast-day" dedicated to Marduk and Zarpanitu, which Sayce calls "a day of rest (Sabbath)". Restrictions on the king: he must not eat meat cooked over a fire or in smoke, change his clothes, put on white garments, offer sacrifice, ride in his chariot or issue royal decrees; the diviner must not give a secret oracle; no medicine for the body; not a day for cursing. At night the king makes his offering before Marduk and Ishtar.
